The Blue Innovator of Veldoria
By EMMETT McDOWELL

Innovation was Mila Little's stock in trade, and every corporate boardroom had known her touch. But now, on Veldoria, she was selling her expertise into the weirdest of all her exploits—gambling her reputation against the soft promises of sustainable profit.

On the stage of the Havenbrook Innovation Summit, a sharp-dressed, quick-witted brunette was presenting "The Future of Conscious Commerce." The presentation was a bold, revolutionary pitch, a favorite of the entrepreneurs and venture capitalists, the tech pioneers and industry leaders who frequented the summit. The woman delivered it with such conviction that the audience burst into enthusiastic applause.

She bent her head in acknowledgment so that her dark hair fell forward. There was determination in her expression. Her professional smile was practiced. Her eyes were calculating.

The man who had been managing the presentation tech sat at the side of the stage, his back to the crowded auditorium. He did not look up at the presenter but kept his pale, nervous face bent over the control panel, while his fingers lightly, automatically adjusted the displays. Sweat trickled down the back of his neck, plastering his shirt to his back. Without looking up, he said: "Have you spotted him?" His voice was pitched to reach the presenter alone.

The woman, with an almost imperceptible gesture, shook her head.

The conference room was climate-controlled; but then everything is controlled on Veldoria, the newest, the most regulated, the most scrutinized of Earth's economic frontiers. Ventilation systems throughout the building efficiently circulated the air, while the men and women sitting in the auditorium drank heavily of Synth-Tea, the pale blue beverage of Veldoria. Only the native staff, the enigmatic, sharp-eyed Veldorians, seemed unaffected by the tension. They didn't show stress at all.

Up on the stage the presenter was about to begin another segment when she stiffened.

"Here he is," she said to the tech manager without moving her lips.

The tech manager swung around on his stool, lifted his dark eyes to the entrance leading to the main corridor.

Just within the doorway, a tall, thin man was standing. He looked like a gaunt gray wolf loitering in the entrance. His tailored suit hung perfectly. His silver hair was precisely styled, his nose thin and aristocratic. For a moment he studied the crowded auditorium before making his way to a vacant seat in the back row.

"Continue," said the tech manager in a flat voice.

The brunette shivered. Stepping from the stage she made her way through the rows until she came to the seat occupied by the newcomer.

"May I join you?" she asked in a low voice.

The man stood. "Of course. I was expecting you. Here, sit down." He gestured to the adjacent seat, motioned for a server. The Veldorian, his sharp observant eyes missing nothing, approached smoothly. "Bring us two Synth-Teas from the Glendale Region, chilled." The server glided away.

"So," said the brunette; "you came. I wasn't certain you would arrive in time." Her hands were clenched in her lap. The knuckles were white.

The man said nothing.

"I didn't want to bring you in, Mila Little." It was the first time she had used her name. "You have the reputation of being unpredictable. I don't trust you, but since..." She stopped as the server placed glasses on the tray table and deftly poured the pale blue beverage. The woman, Mila Little, raised her glass.

"Here's to environmental ethics," she said. Her low voice carried an odd, compelling note. Her eyes, pale blue and amused, were calculating against her tanned face.

The brunette drew in her breath.

"No! Veldoria isn't ready for full sustainability. Only a handful of idealists are pushing the transformation. The real business leaders are against it, but they're afraid to protest publicly. You've got to believe me. The transformation is scheduled to launch during the Global Innovation Forum. If it does, the traditional corporations here will be destroyed. The Veldorians have been planning this. We have only a handful of allies."

Mila Little wiped the condensation from her glass with a fine napkin. "I had forgotten how intensely competitive it can be here."

The brunette ignored the interruption. "There is one person; she is the leader, the very soul of the transformation movement. The Veldorians follow her completely. They will do whatever she says. Without her they would be lost. She is the reformer, Rachel Rogers. I am to offer you ten thousand credits to discredit Rachel Rogers."

Mila Little refilled their empty glasses. She was a striking woman, elegant in a sharp fashion. Only her eyes were different. They were flat and a trifle oblique with straight brows. The pupils were a pale and penetrating blue that could analyze like a forensic accountant. Now she caught the brunette's eyes and held them with her own as a lawyer pins a witness.

"Why call me all the way from Nordavia for that? Why not have that tech manager at the panel handle Rogers?"

The brunette started, glanced at the tech manager, said with a shiver: "We can't locate Rachel Rogers. Don't look at me that way, Mila. You frighten me. I'm telling the truth. We can't find her. That's why we called you. You've got to find her, Mila. She's transforming all of Veldoria."

"Who's putting up the money?"

"I can't tell you."

"Ah," said Mila Little; "so that's the way it is."

"That's the way it is."

"There isn't much time," she said after a moment. "The Forum is in just days."

"No," the brunette replied. "But we think she's here in Havenbrook."

"Why? What makes you think that?"

"She was seen," she began, then stopped with a gasp.

The lights had gone out.

It was as unexpected as a data breach. One moment the auditorium was glowing in light, the next the darkness swooped down on the attendees, pressing against their eyes like black velvet. The ventilation systems slowed audibly and stopped. It grew warmer, closer.

Mila Little slipped sideways from her seat. She felt something brush her sleeve. Somewhere someone gasped.

"What's happening here?" growled a petulant male voice. Other voices took up the complaint.

Across from Mila there was the sense of movement; she could detect it. An exclamation was suddenly choked off as if a hand had been placed over the brunette's mouth.

"Melissa!" said Mila in a low voice.

There was no answer.

"Melissa!" she repeated, louder.

Unexpectedly, the deep, authoritative voice of the Summit Director boomed out from the stage.

"It's all right. The main circuit breaker tripped. The lights will be on in a moment."

Following his announcement the lights flashed on, driving the darkness upward. The ventilation systems recommenced their quiet humming.

Mila Little glanced at her seat. The brunette presenter was gone. So was the tech manager.

Mila Little sat quietly back down and poured herself another glass of Synth-Tea. The pale blue beverage had a subtle yet energizing taste. It made her think of clarity and focus. In the intense, competitive environment of Veldoria it was as refreshing as a strategic breakthrough.

She wondered who was putting up the ten thousand credits? Who stood to lose most in case of a successful transformation? The answer seemed obvious enough. Who, but Michael Gardner. Gardner controlled the traditional manufacturing sector for which there was tremendous demand throughout the system.

And what had happened to Melissa Herrera. Had the reformers abducted her? If so, she suspected they had caught someone formidable. Melissa had the reputation of being able to handle herself.

She beckoned a server, settled her bill. As the Veldorian started to leave, a thought struck Mila. These sharp-eyed Veldorians could read situations as well as any trained psychologist. For generations they had lived by understanding social dynamics and reading between the lines. She peeled off a bill, put it in the server's hands.

"What became of the brunette presenter?"

The Veldorian glanced at the bill, then back at the consultant. There was no readable expression in his sharp eyes.

"She and the man, the nervous one who managed the tech, slipped out the exit to the corridor."

Mila shrugged, dismissed the server. She had not expected to get much information from him, but she was not a woman to overlook any possibility. If Melissa had been abducted, only Veldorians could have engineered it in the dark; and the Veldorians were a tight-knit community.

Back in the narrow corridor Mila Little headed for her hotel. The walls were lined with promotional materials for sustainable business initiatives and consciousness studies programs. Beneath her feet, she knew, stretched a network of underground facilities and passages. Somewhere in those corporate mazes was Rachel Rogers, the reformer, and Melissa.

At regular intervals blue-tinted lights illuminated the passage, casting a clinical glow. She had just passed one of these lights when she thought she detected a footfall behind her. It was only the whisper of a sound, but as she passed beyond the circle of light, she pressed herself against the wall. Nothing stirred. There was no further sound. Again she started forward, but now she was conscious of shadows following her. They were never visible, but to her trained senses there came subtle, revealing signs: the brush of fabric against the smooth walls, the careful placement of steps. She ducked down a connecting corridor, faded into a doorway. Immediately all sounds of pursuit stopped. But as soon as she emerged she was conscious again of the followers. In the controlled, monitored environment, she was like a novice trying to elude the perceptive Veldorians.

In the distance a soft glow indicated the approach of dawn. The Veldorian sunrise was about to break. With an oath, she set out again for her hotel. She made no further effort to elude the followers.

Once back in her room, Mila Little removed her jacket, checked a concealed recording device, activated her security system. Her body language was tense and marked by years of high-stakes negotiations. There were subtle signs of stress and long hours, and her left wrist bore the unmistakable mark of carpal tunnel from years of typing reports. Stepping to the window, she surveyed the city, then returned to activate her communication device. The device was sophisticated with advanced encryption. Next she reviewed her notes and stretching out on the chair began to contemplate her strategy with singular focus.

She had, she supposed, disrupted rather a lot of businesses. She had fought in the brutal consulting wars of the Nordavia markets for years, then the Universal Financial Crisis of 2068, after that the Pinehurst Transformation as well as dozens of smaller engagements between competing firms. No, there was little doubt but that she had disrupted quite a number of established businesses. But this matter of tracking a reformer through the corporate networks beneath the city was outside her usual scope.

Furthermore, there was something suspicious about the entire setup. The Veldorians, she knew, had been advocating for sustainable practices for years. Why, at this time when the Global Council was about to mandate environmental ethics standards, would they stage a radical transformation?

A loud, authoritative knock at the door interrupted further analysis. She stood and deactivated her notes. Before she could reach the door the knocking came again.

Checking the security screen, she opened the door cautiously.

"Come in," she called.

The door swung open. A heavy-set man entered, closed and locked the door, then glanced around carefully. His eyes fastened on Mila. He cleared his throat nervously.

"Ms. Little, the—ah—business consultant, I believe." His voice was measured, almost rehearsed. "I'm Michael Gardner." He held out a manicured hand.

Mila said nothing. She ignored the hand, waited, alert.

Mr. Gardner cleared his throat again. "I have come, Ms. Little, on a matter of business, urgent business. I had not intended to appear in this matter. I preferred to remain behind the scenes, but the disappearance of Ms. Herrera has—ah—forced my hand." He paused.

Mila still said nothing. Ms. Herrera must be the brunette presenter, whom at different times she had known under several different professional identities. She doubted that even Melissa remembered her original company affiliation.

"Ms. Herrera made you a proposition?" Michael Gardner's voice was tight.

"Yes," said Mila.

"You accepted?"

"Why, no. As it happened she was abducted before I had the chance."

Mr. Gardner's jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. "That's most unfortunate. Ms. Herrera has been with me for seven years. She started as an intern, you know. I sponsored her through the certification program myself." He paused, cleared his throat. "But the fact remains that unless Rachel Rogers is stopped immediately there will be a complete industry collapse all over the region during the Global Innovation Forum. The Council doesn't realize the seriousness of the situation."

"Then I was right; it is you who are putting up the ten thousand credits."

"Not entirely," said Gardner uncomfortably. "There are many of us here, Veldorians as well as off-worlders, who recognize the danger. We have—ah—pooled our resources."

"But you stand to lose most in case of a successful transformation?"

"Perhaps. I have a large stake in traditional manufacturing. It is—ah—lucrative. But Ms. Little, I also employ over three thousand workers in this region. Many of them are Veldorians who have worked for my family for generations. A collapse would devastate their communities."

Mila Little activated her recording device discreetly, sat down on the edge of the chair. "Why beat around the bush," she asked with a sudden smile. "Mr. Gardner, you've gained control of the manufacturing sector. Other off-worlders control the mining operations and the northern agricultural zones. Together you form perhaps the strongest combine the system has ever seen. You actually run Veldoria's economy, and you've extracted every possible profit. Every time sustainability standards have come before the Global Council you've succeeded in blocking them. You are, perhaps, the most unpopular group anywhere. I don't wonder that you fear a transformation movement."

Mr. Gardner took out a handkerchief and mopped his forehead. "Fifteen thousand credits I can offer you. But no more. That is as high as I can go."

Mila laughed. "How did you know Melissa had been taken?"

"We have a very efficient information network. I had the report of Ms. Herrera's abduction fifteen minutes after the fact. I sent Li immediately to ensure her safety, but he couldn't locate her."

Mila raised her eyebrows. "Perhaps then you know where she is?"

Mr. Gardner shook his head. "No. Rachel Rogers' people took her."

A second knock at the door caused them to exchange glances. Mila went to the door, checked the security screen, opened it. The tech manager from the summit was in the doorway. His dark eyes were intense in his pale nervous face. His shirt was rumpled with sweat and stress.

"They told me Mr. Gardner was here," he said.

"It's for you," said Mila over her shoulder.

Mr. Gardner came to the door. His face softened slightly. "Li. Thank goodness you're safe. I was worried when I heard Rogers' people were in the area. Where's Ms. Herrera?"

"I couldn't reach her. Look, Mr. Gardner, I need to see you alone."

Michael Gardner said, "Would you excuse me, Ms. Little?" He cleared his throat. "I'll just step out into the hall a moment." He went out, drawing the door shut after him.

Mila activated another recording device. She reviewed her notes nervously, checking data on her tablet. She sat down on the edge of the chair. She stood up and closed the tablet. She went to the door, but did not open it. Instead, she took another look at her security feeds. Again she came to a halt before the door, activated the audio sensor. For a long time she listened but could distinguish no murmur of voices. With an oath she opened the door. The hall was empty.

II

Mila returned to her room, gathered her equipment, checked her security system. She tested the recording device. It was a sophisticated, powerful tool which captured every detail. She preferred it because, though she rarely used information destructively, it provided comprehensive documentation. She adjusted the device carefully to ensure it wouldn't malfunction if she needed it urgently. Then she went out into the hall.

At the front desk she inquired if any messages had come for her. There were none, but the clerk had seen Mr. Gardner with a young man take the elevator to the underground facilities. Above the clerk's head a news display was streaming current events in real-time. Mila read:

"Global Council suspends negotiations on Veldorian sustainability standards pending investigation of rumored radical transformation. Off-worlders advised to return home. Rachel Rogers, Veldorian reformer, being sought."

Mila descended to the network of underground facilities which served as the business district during peak hours. Here in the lower levels were located the offices and meeting rooms where the Veldorians conducted their affairs, sitting around conference tables discussing quietly the future of sustainable business. The facilities were efficiently lit, the natives preferring the controlled environment, and Mila had to navigate carefully, passing by the observant, silent populace. But when she reached the off-world quarter of the city, bright commercial lighting took place of the efficient blue-tinted lights, and there was a sprinkling of security personnel among the crowd.

Mila halted before a door bearing a placard which read:

"GARDNER MANUFACTURING TRUST"

She pushed through the door into a professionally decorated reception area. At the far end was a second door beside which sat a desk, door and desk being separated from the rest of the office by a glass partition. The door into Michael Gardner's inner office was slightly ajar. Mila could distinguish voices; then quite clearly she heard Michael Gardner say in a measured tone:

"Li, I thought I left you in the native quarter. Why did you follow me? How many times have I told you the native quarter isn't safe right now? Rogers' people are everywhere."

The reply was unintelligible. Then the pale-faced young man came through the door closing it after himself. At the sight of Mila Little he froze.

"What are you doing here?"

Mila settled herself warily, her pale blue eyes assessing the young man.

"Let's get this straight," she said calmly. "I've known your type before. Frankly, ever since I saw you I've had to suppress an urge to report you for corporate espionage."

The young man's dark eyes were intense, his hands twitching. His hands began to move toward his pocket.

"You interfering..." he began, but he got no further. Mila Little activated her recording device audibly.

The sophisticated recording device seemed to appear in Mila's hand. The clear audio capture made the young man freeze against the wall. Mila calmly continued recording.

"I'll ruin you for this," said Li, his expression twisted with anger. "You've destroyed my cover. I'll destroy your reputation."

The door to the inner office swung open.

"What's happened?" cried Michael Gardner in distress. "What's wrong, Li? Are you hurt?"

"This consultant is recording everything."

"But how much?" Gardner was wringing his hands.

"Enough," said Mila. "He'll have his career compromised for a while. That's all."

"Li," said Mr. Gardner, his voice suddenly gentle despite the chaos. "You're creating problems all over my office. Why can't you go to the conference room. There's privacy there, and the medical kit if you need it. I noticed you favoring your left arm earlier." He turned to scan the room. "Where's Ms. Santos? Ms. Santos! Oh, Ms. Santos! That assistant. Ms. Santos!"

Li retreated through a door on the left just as a tall blonde hurried in from the right. She had straight blonde hair which hung to her shoulders, and bright green eyes, and enough professional presence to absorb Mila's attention.

"Oh!" exclaimed Ms. Santos as she caught sight of the tense situation.

"There's been an—ah—incident," said Mr. Gardner, and he cleared his throat. "Call security, Ms. Santos."

Ms. Santos raised an eyebrow, went to the communication panel. In a moment she had connected with the professional figure of a security officer at a desk.

"Could security come right over here? There's been an incident."

"Come over where?" said the officer in the display. "These systems aren't telepathic, ma'am."

"Oh," said Ms. Santos, "the offices of the Gardner Manufacturing Trust."

The officer in the display became more attentive. "I'm sure security can respond. They'll be there momentarily."

"Thank you," said Ms. Santos. She deactivated the panel, then added quietly: "Bureaucrat."

Mr. Gardner regarded Mila Little with distress.

"Really, Ms. Little, was it necessary to record Li? Isn't that—ah—a little extreme? The boy has been through enough. He lost his entire family in the Pinehurst collapse, you know. I've been trying to help him rebuild his life."

"Oh," cried Ms. Santos, her green eyes flashing. "Did you record that young man? Aren't you the aggressive consultant?"

"Young man?" said Mila calmly. "Dangerous corporate spy. I documented his activities." She held out the recording device. "You take it, Mr. Gardner. Frankly, this gives me leverage. It might be useful."

Mr. Gardner accepted the device reluctantly. He held it as if it might erase any minute. He started to put it in his pocket, thought better of it, glanced around helplessly.

"Here, Ms. Santos," he said, "do something with this. Put it in my safe."

Ms. Santos's eyes grew wide. "I wouldn't touch that device for all the manufacturing contracts on Veldoria."

"Here, I'll take it," said Li coming back into the room. He had composed himself somewhat. His face was even paler, if possible. Mila eyed him coldly as with his hand the young man took the recording device.

"Act like you want to use that information and I'll expose everything next time."

"Now, Ms. Little." Mr. Gardner cleared his throat nervously. "Li, go into my office and rest. Security will be here in a moment. Ms. Santos, you may leave early. I'll have no more work for you today. And please," he added, "take the service corridor. I don't want any of my people running into Rogers' operatives."

Michael Gardner led Li through the door. Mila and Ms. Santos were alone. With her eye on the door, Mila said:

"When you leave, head toward the native quarter. Wait for me in the first café you come to."

Ms. Santos raised her eyebrows. "What's this? Corporate intrigue?"

"Look," began Mila seriously.

"My eyes are already wide open," she interrupted. "Another morning like this and I take the first transport back to Nordavia." She grabbed her bag from the desk drawer.

"I'm not trying to recruit you carelessly. This is..."

"How disappointing."

Mila began again patiently. "Wait for me in the first café. There's something I must know. It's important." She cleared her throat. "Don't you find the corporate culture rather intense, Ms. Santos. But perhaps you've become accustomed to it."

Mr. Gardner came back into the room.

"Why, no, I mean yes," replied Ms. Santos, a blank expression on her face.

"Goodbye, Ms. Santos," said Mr. Gardner firmly. "And Stella—be careful out there."

Mila smiled slightly at her. Ms. Santos left the room looking confused.

As the door closed behind the assistant, Michael Gardner cleared his throat, said: "Ms. Little, I suppose my disappearance back at your hotel requires some explanation. But the fact is that Li brought an important piece of information." He paused.

Mila said nothing.

"You might be interested to know that Ms. Herrera is quite safe. Rachel Rogers has her, but Li assures me she will be quite safe." Again he paused. As Mila remained silent, his neck flushed.

"The fact is, Ms. Little, that we won't need you after all. I realize that we've put you to considerable trouble and we're prepared to pay you whatever you believe your time is worth. Say five hundred credits?"

"That's fair enough," replied Mila.

Michael Gardner sighed. "I have the payment authorization ready."

"Only," continued Mila coldly, "I'm not ready to be bought off. I think I'll investigate this situation further."

Mr. Gardner's face fell. "You won't reconsider? Ms. Little, I'm asking you to leave this alone. For your own safety, and for the safety of people who don't deserve to be caught in the crossfire."

"Sorry," said Mila; "but I have an appointment. I'm late now." She started to leave.

"Li!" called Michael Gardner.

The pale-faced young man appeared in the doorway, a data device in his hand. Mila Little stepped back quickly, activating her recording device as she moved. There was a tiny click as Li activated something. She heard the whisper of data transmission. Then she began recording openly.

Li stopped, looking uncertain.

Mila maintained her position, keeping awareness of Michael Gardner, documented everything carefully.

"You've compromised him," said Gardner, his voice strained. "If I were you, Ms. Little, I would be on the next transport back to Nordavia. This situation is more dangerous than you realize."

Without answering, Mila backed watchfully from the room.

Once Mila Little had regained the corridor, she reviewed her recordings carefully. Whatever was going on, these people played seriously. Warily she started down the passage toward the native quarter. At the first underground café she entered. Her eyes swept the space, then she smiled.

At a corner table, a tall glass of Synth-Tea before her, sat Ms. Santos. Her blonde hair was slightly disheveled, and she was perched on the edge of her chair as if ready to leave at any moment.

"Surprise," said Mila coming up behind her.

Ms. Santos jumped slightly, then relaxed. She regarded her cautiously.

"Never a boring moment," she said.

Still smiling, Mila sat down. "I'm Mila Little, Ms. Santos. I think Michael Gardner forgot to introduce us properly. There's some questionable business going on here that I'm particularly interested in investigating. I thought you might be able to help me."

"Yes," replied Ms. Santos carefully.

A native server, attracted by their presence, came over and took Mila's order.

"All right," Mila said, but her pale blue eyes studied the assistant thoughtfully. "I'll have to share certain information which might be risky for you to know. Are you willing, Ms. Santos?"

"Since we're going to be colleagues," she replied; "you might begin by calling me Stella. You make me feel overly formal."

"Well then," she said. "In the first place, I just documented that young operative your boss had in his office."

"Oh my," said Stella, surprised.

"It was necessary," she hastened to explain. "He was involved in corporate espionage with that data device."

"But the authorities!" she cried.

"There'll never be an investigation. Michael Gardner will ensure that. I was called here on what I supposed was a legitimate consulting engagement. Instead I was offered ten thousand credits to discredit the leader of the transformation movement."

"What transformation? I'm confused."

"The Veldorians, of course."

"I don't believe it," said Stella. "The Veldorians are the most principled people in the system. They've been advocating for sustainability, yes. But they believe in ethical business practices. I don't believe you could induce a Veldorian to engage in corporate sabotage, even in self-defense. That's why Michael Gardner and the rest of the combine had such an easy time gaining control of the manufacturing sector."

"Exactly," breathed Mila, "I begin to understand. Stella—I've a notion that we're going to work well together. How do you happen to be Michael Gardner's assistant?"

"A woman needs employment. I'll say this—Gardner pays better than anyone else in the sector. Three times what the sustainable firms offer for the same position."

Mila Little raised her oblique brows but did not interrupt.

"The benefits are extraordinary," Stella continued, swirling her Synth-Tea. "Full medical coverage, retirement contributions, even education stipends. Last month he approved emergency leave for a warehouse supervisor whose daughter was ill—full pay for six weeks. And when the Thornton family lost their home in the eastern floods, Gardner personally funded their relocation."

"Generous," said Mila neutrally.

"Some would say so. Others..." Stella paused, her green eyes flickering. "There was an incident three years ago. A young engineer named Dara Okonkwo discovered irregularities in the supply chain—evidence that Gardner Manufacturing was falsifying environmental compliance records. She brought it to Gardner directly, trusting in his reputation."

"What happened?"

"Gardner thanked her warmly. Expressed deep concern. Promised a full internal investigation." Stella's voice had gone flat. "Two days later, Okonkwo's security clearance was revoked. Within a week, she'd been transferred to a remote monitoring station in the northern territories. Within a month, she resigned. The official reason was 'personal circumstances.' I processed the paperwork myself."

Mila leaned forward. "And the irregularities?"

"Never mentioned again. The compliance records remained unchanged. Gardner's quarterly profits that year broke company records."

"Yet he approved emergency leave for the warehouse supervisor."

"Six weeks later, that same supervisor testified before the Regional Labor Board that working conditions at Gardner Manufacturing were exemplary. His testimony helped defeat a unionization effort that would have cost the company millions in increased wages."

Mila's pale eyes narrowed. "So the generosity..."

"Is selective," Stella said carefully. "I've watched him for three years. When old Marcus Chen retired—forty years of service—Gardner threw him a lavish party. Speeches about loyalty and family. Then I discovered that Chen's pension had been quietly reduced by forty percent due to a 'calculation error' that was never corrected."

"Did Chen know?"

"He's eighty-two years old and half-blind. He trusted Gardner to handle the details." Stella's hands tightened around her glass. "When I asked Gardner about it, he said the pension fund was under stress and difficult choices had to be made. He seemed genuinely pained by the situation. Said it kept him up at night."

"But he didn't restore the pension."

"He bought Chen a very expensive retirement gift instead. A antique timepiece worth perhaps five hundred credits. The pension shortfall costs Chen three thousand credits annually."

Mila sat back, processing. "You said the Gardner Manufacturing Trust is in financial trouble?"

"The stock has been dropping precipitously," Stella confirmed. "Traditional manufacturing can't compete with sustainable alternatives anymore. Not since the Global Council started pushing environmental standards."

"What has Gardner done about it?"

"That's what I've been trying to understand." Stella leaned closer, lowering her voice. "Three months ago, I noticed a pattern in the financial records. Large transfers to shell companies, all registered in jurisdictions with minimal oversight. I started keeping notes."

"Did you confront him?"

"I'm not that foolish. I've seen what happens to people who confront Michael Gardner." Stella paused. "But I did overhear something. Last week, Gardner was on a secured call. He thought I'd left for the day. He said something about 'the transformation timeline' and 'positioning for maximum return.' Then he laughed and said, 'Rogers understands the arrangement perfectly.'"

"Rachel Rogers? The reformer he's paying me to discredit?"

"The same." Stella's green eyes were troubled. "It makes no sense unless..."

"Unless they're working together," Mila finished. "Creating a crisis to profit from the solution."

"That's what I've begun to suspect. But there's something else." Stella hesitated. "Li—the young tech manager. Do you know how he came to work for Gardner?"

"I assumed he was hired normally."

"Three years ago, Li was destitute. His family's business collapsed during the Pinehurst economic crisis—a crisis, I might add, that Gardner Manufacturing profited from substantially through strategic acquisitions. Li was about to be deported when Gardner personally intervened. Sponsored his visa, gave him a position, even helped him find housing."

"Sounds generous."

"It was. Everyone said so. Li himself credits Gardner with saving his life." Stella's voice dropped lower. "But Li is also the one who handles Gardner's most sensitive communications. He has access to financial systems that even I can't see. And whenever there's something questionable happening—like the Okonkwo situation, or the compliance irregularities—Li is always nearby, always loyal, always ready to do whatever Gardner asks."

Mila considered this. "You're suggesting Li's loyalty was... cultivated. Deliberately."

"I'm suggesting that Michael Gardner never does anything without considering its utility." Stella finished her Synth-Tea. "Three years I've worked for him. I've seen him weep genuine tears over a worker's family tragedy and then cut that same worker's overtime the following month to meet profit targets. I've watched him mentor young employees with apparent sincerity while positioning them for roles that serve his interests. I've heard him speak passionately about his responsibility to the Veldorian community while his lawyers find new ways to minimize his tax obligations."

"So which is real? The concern or the calculation?"

Stella was quiet for a long moment. "When I first started, I believed he genuinely cared. The way he remembered everyone's names, asked about their families, seemed to feel their struggles..." She shook her head slowly. "But I've watched too many patterns repeat. The public generosity followed by private cost-cutting. The expressed concern followed by convenient inaction. The rescued employees who become the most useful tools."

"You think he's deliberately deceptive?"

"I think," Stella said carefully, "that he's learned exactly which expressions of concern pay dividends and which ones don't. But I can't prove what's in his heart. No one can. All I can tell you is what I've observed: the kindnesses that cost him little and gain him much, the concerns that never quite translate into financial sacrifice, the loyalty he cultivates in people who then serve his purposes."

Mila Little smiled grimly. "Then we need to find Rachel Rogers and Melissa Herrera. And we need to do it before the Global Innovation Forum."

"I know where Rogers might be," Stella said hesitantly. "There's a consciousness studies research facility in the Pinehurst district. It's funded by several sustainable business initiatives. If she's orchestrating this transformation, that's where she'd be coordinating from."

"Then that's where we're going," Mila said, standing. "Are you with me?"

Stella Santos looked at her empty glass of Synth-Tea, then at the determined consultant. "I suppose a woman needs adventure too. Let's go."

Together they left the café, heading into the underground passages toward Pinehurst, where the truth about Veldoria's transformation—and Michael Gardner's real priorities—waited to be uncovered.
